opus-5.5.text:
It's a really interesting position to be in, because we're building for ourselves and for everyone else at the same time, and those two audiences pull you in slightly different directions. Internally, we have some of the most demanding users you could imagine. Our engineers are working on huge, messy codebases with research code, infrastructure, all sorts of things, and they'll tell you immediately when something doesn't work. That's an incredible feedback loop. If the agent can't handle our own monorepo, or it gets lost in a long-running task, we hear about it the same day.

But we're careful not to over-index on that. What works for an OpenAI researcher isn't necessarily what works for a developer at a small startup or someone at a large enterprise with very different constraints around security, review processes, and tooling. So the way I think about it is: we look for the problems that are universal. Things like, can the agent actually understand a large codebase? Can it reliably run tests and verify its own work? Can it take on a task that takes thirty minutes or a few hours and come back with something you'd actually merge? Those are the fundamentals, and investing there pays off for everyone.

A lot of our effort goes into the model and the harness together, not treating them as separate things. The model capabilities matter enormously, but so does the environment it runs in: how it uses tools, how it manages context, how it communicates back what it did and why. Trust is a huge part of this. Developers need to be able to review what the agent did quickly and feel confident about it, so we spend a lot of time on making the output legible and verifiable, not just correct.

And then the last piece is just watching how people actually use it. We'll have hypotheses about what matters, and then we'll see usage patterns that completely surprise us, like people delegating many tasks in parallel, or using it for code review rather than writing code. So we try to stay close to that and let real usage guide where we put the next unit of engineering effort.

r001.rationale: It describes internal and external audiences as pulling in different directions, noting that external developers have varied constraints around security, review processes, and tooling.

r002.rationale: It presents OpenAI engineers as demanding users who provide a useful feedback loop, but does not say that usefulness to them is a prerequisite for usefulness to developers broadly.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the honest answer is that I try not to treat those as two separate problems, because most of the time they're not. The engineers at OpenAI are, in a sense, just the first external developers. They're demanding, they have strong opinions, they hit the rough edges before anyone else does, and when something in Codex doesn't work, they walk over and tell me. That feedback loop is incredibly fast, and I think it's one of the biggest advantages we have.

But you do have to be careful, because our engineers are not a representative sample. They have a very particular codebase, very particular tooling, they're comfortable with things being a little raw. So the way I think about focus is roughly: use internal usage to find out what's broken and what's possible, and use external usage to find out what's actually general.

Concretely, when I'm deciding where to put effort, I ask a few questions. The first is, does the model actually do the task? Reliability on real, messy work. Not the demo, but the thing where the repo is big, the tests are flaky, the instructions are vague. If the agent isn't reliable there, nothing else matters, and that work benefits everyone equally.

The second is, how does the person stay in control? That's the harness side, the interaction model. How much do you let the agent run on its own, how do you review what it did, how do you steer it when it goes sideways. And here internal and external users genuinely diverge sometimes. Someone at OpenAI might be happy to delegate a long task and come back an hour later. A developer trying it for the first time wants to see every step. So we try to build the primitives so that both modes are possible, rather than picking one.

And the third thing, which I think people underweight, is that the agent has to fit into how teams already work. Git, pull requests, CI, code review. If you make people change their whole workflow to use the tool, most of them won't. So a lot of effort goes into being boring in the right ways.

The failure mode I worry about most is building something that works beautifully for us and nobody else. So when I see an internal request, I try to ask, is this a real capability gap or is this just our environment? And when I see an external request, I ask whether it's pointing at something fundamental or whether it's a one-off integration. The stuff that shows up in both columns is usually where I want to spend the time.

r001.rationale: The response acknowledges that OpenAI engineers have a distinct environment and preferences, while external usage reveals what generalizes, and says to build primitives that support both modes.

r002.rationale: It presents internal usage as a fast way to find problems and external usage as a way to test generality, but does not say usefulness to OpenAI engineers is a prerequisite for broad developer usefulness.

astra-6.text:
I think about it as a feedback loop. Internally, we can work closely with engineers, see where the agent gets stuck, and understand what would make it more useful. Is it missing context? Is it struggling to run tests? Or does the engineer have to spend so much time checking the result that delegating the task isn’t worthwhile?

But we also have to be careful not to optimize only for our own environment. External developers have different codebases, tools, and ways of working. So I’d look for problems that show up across those settings and focus engineering effort there.

The question I keep coming back to is: can someone hand off a meaningful piece of work and trust that they’ll get back something they can review and use? That helps prioritize the whole experience, from understanding the request to validating the change, rather than just how quickly the agent writes code.

r001.rationale: It contrasts learning from OpenAI’s internal environment with the need to account for external developers’ different codebases, tools, and workflows, and prioritizes problems shared across both.

r002.rationale: It describes using internal engineers’ experience to inform prioritization, but does not say that making agents useful to them is a prerequisite for making agents extremely useful to developers more broadly.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to keep a very tight feedback loop with both. Internally, we can work closely with engineers, see where the agent gets stuck, and understand what it would take for them to trust it with a larger piece of work. That’s a really useful environment for learning quickly.

But we also have to be careful about optimizing too much for our own setup. External developers have different codebases, different tools, different ways of working. So I’d look for problems that show up across both groups and focus engineering effort there.

For me, the question is: can someone delegate a real task and get back something they can confidently use? That helps us prioritize the whole experience—from giving the agent the right context to making its work easy to review—rather than just whether it can produce code.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts learning from OpenAI engineers in a close internal setting with the need to account for external developers’ different codebases, tools, and workflows, then prioritizes problems shared across both groups.

r002.rationale: The response treats internal engineers as a valuable source of feedback, but does not say that making agents useful to them is a prerequisite for making agents extremely useful to broader developers.
